docs.text: Resolution Description f09_g17 ~1° atmosphere, ~1° ocean f19_g17 ~2° atmosphere, ~1° ocean CLM_USRDAT User-provided data (single-point)

docs.title: Checking Case Status
docs.text:
The CaseStatus file logs all workflow steps:

cat CaseStatus

Look for timestamps and success/failure messages. When a case fails, CaseStatus points to the relevant log file.

docs.title: Run Types
docs.text:
CTSM supports three run types:

Type Use Case Configuration Changes? Bit-for-bit? startup Fresh simulation N/A N/A branch Exact continuation No Yes hybrid New start from restart Yes No

docs.title: Continuing a Run (CONTINUE_RUN)
docs.text:
To continue a run from where it stopped:

./xmlchange CONTINUE_RUN=TRUE
./case.submit

This is the simplest continuation - the run picks up exactly where it left off.

docs.title: Branch Runs
docs.text:
Branch runs continue from another case's restart, maintaining bit-for-bit reproducibility:

cd $CIME_SCRIPTS

# Create new case
./create_newcase \
    --case $CASES/my_branch_case \
    --compset I1850Clm60BgcCrop \
    --res f09_g17 \
    --machine hipergator \
    --run-unsupported

cd $CASES/my_branch_case

# Configure as branch run
./xmlchange RUN_TYPE=branch
./xmlchange RUN_REFCASE=source_case_name
./xmlchange RUN_REFDATE=0005-01-01
./xmlchange RUN_REFDIR=/path/to/source/case/rest/0005-01-01-00000

# TRUE: case.submit stages the restart and rpointer files from RUN_REFDIR into RUNDIR
# FALSE: you must copy them into RUNDIR yourself
./xmlchange GET_REFCASE=TRUE

./case.setup
./case.build
./case.submit

Branch Run Restrictions

Branch runs must use the same compset and resolution as the source case. You cannot change model configuration in a branch run.

docs.title: Hybrid Runs
docs.text:
Hybrid runs initialize from restart files but allow configuration changes:

./xmlchange RUN_TYPE=hybrid
./xmlchange RUN_REFCASE=source_case_name
./xmlchange RUN_REFDATE=0005-01-01
./xmlchange RUN_REFDIR=/path/to/source/case/rest/0005-01-01-00000
./xmlchange GET_REFCASE=TRUE   # FALSE means you stage restart files into RUNDIR yourself

Use hybrid runs when you need to: - Change compset or resolution - Modify namelist settings that affect initialization - Start a new experiment from a spun-up state

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Naming convention: Include compset and date in case names (e.g., I1850Clm60BgcCrop.f09_g17.240115)
  • Check before building: Use ./preview_namelists to verify configuration
  • Don't edit generated files: Modify user_nl_* files, not the generated *_in files
  • Keep case directories: They're small and useful for reproducing runs

docs.title: History Output
docs.text: CTSM writes diagnostic output to history files (NetCDF format). This page covers configuring what variables are output, at what frequency, and how they're averaged.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: History output is configured in user_nl_clm. Changes take effect on the next run (no rebuild required).

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
! Clear default output, add specific variables
hist_empty_htapes = .true.
hist_fincl1 = 'TSA', 'TSKIN', 'GPP', 'EFLX_LH_TOT', 'FSH'

! Daily output, one year per file
hist_nhtfrq = -24
hist_mfilt = 365

docs.title: Key Namelist Variables
docs.text: Variable Purpose Default hist_empty_htapes Clear default output .false. hist_fincl1 - hist_fincl10 Variables for h0-h9 streams varies hist_nhtfrq Output frequency 0 (monthly) hist_mfilt Samples per file 1

docs.title: Output Frequency
docs.text:
The hist_nhtfrq variable controls output frequency:

Value Meaning Example 0 Monthly average Default > 0 Every N timesteps 48 = every 48 timesteps < 0 Every N hours -24 = daily, -1 = hourly

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
! Monthly averages (default)
hist_nhtfrq = 0

! Daily averages
hist_nhtfrq = -24

! 6-hourly output
hist_nhtfrq = -6

! Every timestep (30-min default)
hist_nhtfrq = 1

docs.title: Samples Per File
docs.text:
The hist_mfilt variable sets how many time samples go in each file:

! One year of daily data per file
hist_nhtfrq = -24
hist_mfilt = 365

! One month of daily data per file
hist_nhtfrq = -24
hist_mfilt = 31

! 12 months per file (monthly data)
hist_nhtfrq = 0
hist_mfilt = 12

docs.title: Averaging Flags
docs.text:
By default, variables are averaged over the output period. Append a flag to change this:

Flag Meaning Example A Average (default) 'GPP' or 'GPP:A' I Instantaneous 'TSA:I' M Minimum 'TSA:M' X Maximum 'TSA:X' SUM Sum 'RAIN:SUM' 
! Daily max and min temperature
hist_fincl1 = 'TSA:X', 'TSA:M', 'GPP'

docs.title: Multiple History Streams
docs.text:
You can configure up to 10 independent history streams (h0-h9):

! h0: Monthly averages of key variables
hist_fincl1 = 'GPP', 'NPP', 'NEE', 'TLAI'
hist_nhtfrq(1) = 0
hist_mfilt(1) = 12

! h1: Daily water balance
hist_fincl2 = 'QSOIL', 'QVEGE', 'QVEGT', 'RAIN', 'SNOW'
hist_nhtfrq(2) = -24
hist_mfilt(2) = 365

! h2: Hourly temperature for heat waves
hist_fincl3 = 'TSA', 'TSKIN'
hist_nhtfrq(3) = -1
hist_mfilt(3) = 24

docs.title: Energy Balance
docs.text: Variable Description Units FSH Sensible heat flux W/m² EFLX_LH_TOT Latent heat flux W/m² FSA Absorbed solar radiation W/m² FIRA Net infrared radiation W/m²

docs.title: Carbon Fluxes
docs.text: Variable Description Units GPP Gross primary production gC/m²/s NPP Net primary production gC/m²/s NEE Net ecosystem exchange gC/m²/s ER Ecosystem respiration gC/m²/s

docs.title: Hydrology
docs.text: Variable Description Units QRUNOFF Total runoff mm/s QSOIL Ground evaporation mm/s QVEGE Canopy evaporation mm/s QVEGT Canopy transpiration mm/s TWS Total water storage mm ZWT Water table depth m

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text: Variable Description Units TSA 2m air temperature K TSKIN Surface temperature K TSOI Soil temperature K TV Vegetation temperature K

docs.title: Vegetation
docs.text: Variable Description Units TLAI Total LAI m²/m² TOTVEGC Total vegetation carbon gC/m² TOTSOMC Total soil organic carbon gC/m²

docs.title: Finding Available Variables
docs.text:
List all available history variables:

# Search the history field definitions
grep -r "hist_" $CTSMROOT/bld/namelist_files/

Or check the CTSM documentation: History Fields

docs.title: Output File Naming
docs.text:
History files follow this naming convention:

<case_name>.clm2.h0a.YYYY-MM.nc          # Monthly h0 stream, averaged fields
<case_name>.clm2.h0i.YYYY-MM.nc          # Monthly h0 stream, instantaneous fields
<case_name>.clm2.h1a.YYYY-MM-DD-SSSSS.nc # h1 stream with multiple samples per file

Since ctsm5.3.062, each stream writes averaged (hXa) and instantaneous (hXi) fields to separate files; an hXi file only appears when the stream has instantaneous fields. The date stamp is the time of the file's first sample: YYYY-MM for monthly files with one sample, otherwise YYYY-MM-DD-SSSSS.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start minimal: Begin with hist_empty_htapes = .true. and add only what you need
  • Check file sizes: High-frequency output can generate large files
  • Use multiple streams: Separate high-frequency and low-frequency output
  • Document your choices: Note what variables you're using and why

docs.title: Single-Point Runs
docs.text:
Single-point (site-level) simulations allow you to run CTSM for a specific location rather than a global grid. This is useful for:

  • Validating against tower observations (NEON, FLUXNET)
  • Testing model changes quickly
  • Site-specific research

Single-Point Runs Still Use MPI

Even though single-point runs use only one grid cell, they still require OpenMPI (MPILIB=openmpi) with NTASKS=1. This is because modern CTSM (5.3+) uses ESMF for data model coupling, and ESMF requires a real MPI implementation.

The mpi-serial stub library doesn't work with HiPerGator's ESMF build. See mpi-serial Incompatibility for technical details.

In practice: You still need to submit single-point jobs through SLURM, but they run efficiently on a single core.

docs.title: Subset Data Workflow
docs.text: CTSM provides the subset_data tool to extract site-level data from global datasets.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
subset_data → creates site data → create_newcase with CLM_USRDAT

The subset data creates: - Surface data for the site - Atmospheric forcing data (DATM) - User mods for case configuration

docs.title: Creating Subset Data
docs.text:
cd $CTSMROOT/tools/site_and_regional

# Activate CTSM Python environment
module load conda
conda activate ctsm_pylib

# Run subset_data for a site
./subset_data point \
    --lat 29.6893 \
    --lon -82.0096 \
    --site OSBS \
    --create-surface \
    --create-datm \
    --create-user-mods \
    --datm-syr 2000 \
    --datm-eyr 2020 \
    --outdir $SUBSET_DATA/OSBS

Key arguments:

Argument Description --lat, --lon Site coordinates --site Site name (used in filenames) --create-surface Generate surface data --create-datm Generate atmospheric forcing --create-user-mods Generate the user_mods/ directory used by create_newcase (not created without this flag) --datm-syr, --datm-eyr Forcing data year range (defaults 1901 and 2014) --outdir Output directory

docs.title: Subset Data Output
docs.text:
The tool creates a directory structure:

$SUBSET_DATA/OSBS/
├── surfdata_*.nc           # Surface dataset
├── datmdata/               # Atmospheric forcing
│   └── atm_forcing.*.nc
└── user_mods/
    ├── shell_commands      # XML changes
    ├── user_nl_clm         # CLM namelist additions
    └── user_nl_datm_streams # DATM configuration

docs.title: Creating a Case with Subset Data
docs.text:
cd $CIME_SCRIPTS

./create_newcase \
    --case $CASES/OSBS.I1850Clm60BgcCrop \
    --compset I1850Clm60BgcCrop \
    --res CLM_USRDAT \
    --machine hipergator \
    --run-unsupported \
    --user-mods-dirs $SUBSET_DATA/OSBS/user_mods

Key difference: Use --res CLM_USRDAT and --user-mods-dirs to point to your subset data.

docs.title: Configure and Run
docs.text:
cd $CASES/OSBS.I1850Clm60BgcCrop

# Verify settings (user_mods should have applied changes)
./xmlquery CLM_USRDAT_NAME DATM_MODE

# Setup and build
./case.setup
./case.build

# Modify run length as needed
./xmlchange STOP_OPTION=nyears
./xmlchange STOP_N=5
./xmlchange JOB_WALLCLOCK_TIME=02:00:00

# Submit
./case.submit

docs.title: Available Forcing Data
docs.text:
The fork's default_data_*.cfg files keep upstream's default forcing and change only the input data root (clmforcingindir) to the HiPerGator path:

Dataset Years Used by CRUJRA v2.5 (atm_forcing.datm7.CRUJRA.0.5d.c20241231) 1901-2023 subset_data --create-datm default CRUNCEPv7 (atm_forcing.datm7.cruncep_qianFill.0.5d.v7.c160715) 1901-2016 Our shared OSBS subset data (generated with a custom cfg)

CRUJRA is not in the shared input data

The CRUJRA directory is not currently present under /blue/<group>/earth_models/inputdata/atm/datm7/, so --create-datm with the default cfg fails until it is downloaded. Our existing OSBS subset data was generated from CRUNCEPv7, which is present.

For OSBS specifically, a site-native NEON DATM forcing dataset is also available (2017-02 → 2025-06), produced by an offline fork of the NCAR-NEON pipeline. It is wired in through a user_nl_datm_streams datafiles override rather than --create-datm. See NEON Atmospheric Forcing; note that cycled NEON runs require dtlimit = -1 on the stream (see Troubleshooting).

docs.title: NEON Sites
docs.text:
For NEON tower sites, CTSM provides pre-configured options:

# List available NEON sites
./subset_data point --help

Common sites:

Site Location Ecosystem OSBS Florida Longleaf pine HARV Massachusetts Mixed deciduous BART New Hampshire Northern hardwood

docs.title: Shared Subset Data
docs.text:
Your group may maintain pre-generated subset data for common sites. Check with your group before generating new ones - subset data can be shared to avoid duplicate downloads.

Typical location: /blue/<group>/earth_models/shared.subset.data/

docs.title: subset_data Errors
docs.text: Error Cause Solution "No data found" Coordinates outside data range Verify lat/lon Import errors Missing Python packages Activate ctsm_pylib Path errors Wrong input data location Check $INPUT_DATA

docs.title: Case Errors
docs.text: Error Cause Solution "CLM_USRDAT_NAME not set" user_mods not applied Check --user-mods-dirs path Missing surface data File not found Verify $SUBSET_DATA path

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start small: Run a short test (1 year) before long simulations
  • Check user_mods: After case.setup, verify the settings were applied
  • Keep subset data: It's faster to reuse than regenerate
  • Coordinate precision: Use enough decimal places for your site

docs.title: PTS_MODE (Deprecated)
docs.text: Older documentation may reference PTS_MODE for single-point runs. This is deprecated in CTSM and has limitations (no restart capability). Use the subset data workflow instead.

docs.title: Spinup
docs.text: BGC (biogeochemistry) simulations require spinup to bring soil carbon pools to equilibrium. This process can take hundreds to thousands of simulated years.

docs.title: Why Spinup?
docs.text: Carbon pools in soil take centuries to equilibrate. Starting from arbitrary initial conditions would produce unrealistic results. Spinup runs the model repeatedly until carbon pools stabilize.

docs.title: Two-Phase Spinup
docs.text: CTSM uses a two-phase approach:

docs.title: Phase 1: Accelerated Decomposition (AD) Spinup
docs.text:
Artificially accelerates soil carbon turnover to reach approximate equilibrium faster.

./xmlchange CLM_ACCELERATED_SPINUP=on

Duration: ~200 years is the NCAR guideline (can vary by site). Our OSBS single-point AD spinups ran 600 years (CRUNCEP forcing) and ~195 years (NEON forcing, converged by ~year 180).

docs.title: Phase 2: Post-AD Spinup
docs.text:
Returns to normal decomposition rates and runs to final equilibrium.

./xmlchange CLM_ACCELERATED_SPINUP=off

Duration: Several hundred years

docs.title: 1. Create AD Spinup Case
docs.text:
cd $CIME_SCRIPTS

./create_newcase \
    --case $CASES/my_site.AD_spinup \
    --compset I1850Clm60BgcCrop \
    --res CLM_USRDAT \
    --machine hipergator \
    --run-unsupported \
    --user-mods-dirs $SUBSET_DATA/my_site/user_mods

cd $CASES/my_site.AD_spinup

# Enable accelerated spinup
./xmlchange CLM_ACCELERATED_SPINUP=on

# Run for 200 years
./xmlchange STOP_OPTION=nyears
./xmlchange STOP_N=50
./xmlchange RESUBMIT=3  # 4 submissions × 50 years = 200 years

./case.setup
./case.build
./case.submit

docs.title: 2. Monitor AD Spinup
docs.text:
Check that carbon pools are trending toward equilibrium:

# Look at TOTSOMC (soil organic carbon) over time
# (run from the case directory; history files are archived to DOUT_S_ROOT/lnd/hist)
HIST=$(./xmlquery --value DOUT_S_ROOT)/lnd/hist
ncdump -v TOTSOMC $(ls $HIST/*.clm2.h0a.*.nc | tail -1) | tail

Since ctsm5.3.062, history files are split into averaged (h0a, h1a, ...) and instantaneous (h0i, ...) streams, so look for *.clm2.h0a.*.nc rather than *.clm2.h0.*.nc.

docs.title: 3. Create Post-AD Case
docs.text:
cd $CIME_SCRIPTS

./create_newcase \
    --case $CASES/my_site.postAD_spinup \
    --compset I1850Clm60BgcCrop \
    --res CLM_USRDAT \
    --machine hipergator \
    --run-unsupported \
    --user-mods-dirs $SUBSET_DATA/my_site/user_mods

cd $CASES/my_site.postAD_spinup

# Startup run initialized from the final AD restart
./xmlchange RUN_TYPE=startup
./xmlchange CLM_ACCELERATED_SPINUP=off

# Point finidat at the AD case's last land restart
AD_REST=$(cd $CASES/my_site.AD_spinup && ./xmlquery --value DOUT_S_ROOT)/rest/0201-01-01-00000
echo "finidat = '$AD_REST/my_site.AD_spinup.clm2.r.0201-01-01-00000.nc'" >> user_nl_clm

# Run several hundred years
./xmlchange STOP_OPTION=nyears
./xmlchange STOP_N=100
./xmlchange RESUBMIT=4  # 500 years total

./case.setup
./case.build
./case.submit

Why startup + finidat, not branch

The AD to post-AD transition rescales the soil carbon and nitrogen pools, and that code path only runs when nstep < 2 (SoilBiogeochemCarbonStateType.F90, SoilBiogeochemNitrogenStateType.F90). A branch run keeps the prior case's nstep and fails with "Error in entering/exiting spinup - should occur only when nstep = 1". A startup run with finidat set starts at nstep 1. Our osbs.swenson.post-ad case uses this setup.

docs.title: 4. Check Equilibrium
docs.text:
Spinup is complete when:

  • TOTSOMC, TOTVEGC, TOTECOSYSC are stable year-to-year
  • For global grids, NCAR's criterion is that less than ~3% of the land surface shows carbon disequilibrium. This does not apply to a single-point run.
  • For our single-point site runs we use a block-mean drift test: the change between consecutive 20-year means of TOTECOSYSC, TOTSOMC, and TOTVEGC is below 1%

docs.title: Variables to Monitor
docs.text:
Variable Description TOTECOSYSC Total ecosystem carbon TOTSOMC Soil organic matter carbon TOTVEGC Vegetation carbon GPP Gross primary production TWS Total water storage

Include these in your history output:

hist_fincl1 = 'TOTECOSYSC', 'TOTSOMC', 'TOTVEGC', 'GPP', 'TWS'
hist_nhtfrq = 0  ! Monthly
hist_mfilt = 12  ! 12 months per file

docs.title: Equilibrium Criteria
docs.text:
The model reaches equilibrium when carbon fluxes balance:

  • NEE ≈ 0 (net ecosystem exchange)
  • Carbon pool drift below the thresholds in Check Equilibrium

Arctic and boreal regions take longest (~1000 years).

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start with AD: Never skip AD spinup for BGC runs
  • Check frequently: Don't run hundreds of years without checking progress
  • Save restarts: Keep restart files at key points
  • Site-specific duration: Some sites equilibrate faster than others
  • SP mode doesn't need spinup: Satellite phenology runs don't have prognostic carbon

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution Carbon still drifting Not enough spinup time Continue running Oscillating values Numerical issues Check for extreme climate Very slow equilibration Cold/wet sites Normal for arctic/boreal

docs.title: Satellite Phenology (SP) Mode
docs.text:
If you don't need prognostic carbon pools, SP mode skips the carbon cycle entirely:

--compset I1850Clm60Sp  # No BGC, no spinup needed

SP runs use prescribed LAI from satellite observations and don't require spinup.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Guide to diagnosing and fixing common CTSM failures on HiPerGator.

docs.title: First Steps
docs.text:
When a case fails:

  1. Check CaseStatus - The CaseStatus file in your case directory logs all workflow steps with timestamps. Look for error messages and paths to log files.

  2. Follow the path - CaseStatus points to the specific log containing the error. Read that file.

  3. Check SLURM output - Look for slurm-*.out files in the case directory.

cd $CASES/my_case
cat CaseStatus | tail -20

docs.title: NODE_FAIL
docs.text:
Message: Job <job_id> failed, node failure

Cause: Hardware/system failure on compute node.

Solution: Resubmit the job. If persistent, contact HiPerGator support.

docs.title: TIMEOUT
docs.text:
Message: Job <job_id> cancelled at <timestamp> because it expired

Cause: Job exceeded wall time limit.

Solution: 

./xmlchange JOB_WALLCLOCK_TIME=08:00:00
./case.submit

Or reduce run length with STOP_N.

docs.title: OUT_OF_MEMORY
docs.text:
Message: Job <job_id> killed due to out-of-memory

Cause: Exceeded memory allocation.

Solution: Request more memory or reduce domain size.

docs.title: FAILED (Exit Code)
docs.text:
Message: Job <job_id> failed with exit code <X>

Cause: Model crash - segfault, missing file, numerical error.

Solution: Check the component log files (see below).

docs.title: Finding Log Files
docs.text:
# Query run directory
RUNDIR=$(./xmlquery --value RUNDIR)

# List logs by modification time (most recent first)
ls -t $RUNDIR/*.log.*

docs.title: Key Log Files
docs.text: Log Contains cesm.log.* Top-level model output lnd.log.* Land (CLM) component messages med.log.* Mediator (CMEPS) output, timing info drv.log.* Driver output, run summary atm.log.* Atmosphere (DATM) messages

docs.title: Searching for Errors
docs.text:
# Search all logs for errors
cd $RUNDIR
grep -i "error\|abort\|fail" *.log.* | head -50

# Check end of land log
tail -100 lnd.log.*

docs.title: Did It Fail or Time Out?
docs.text:
Check if all log files were modified at the same time:

cd $RUNDIR
stat *.log.* | grep Modify

If times are within seconds of each other, it likely timed out (the job was killed while running). If times vary, the model crashed.

docs.title: Missing Input Files
docs.text:
Symptom: Error about file not found in lnd.log

Solution: Check paths in namelists, verify input data exists: 

ls $INPUT_DATA/path/to/file

docs.title: Namelist Errors
docs.text:
Symptom: Error parsing namelist in lnd.log

Solution: Check user_nl_clm for syntax errors. Run: 

./preview_namelists

docs.title: Numerical Instability
docs.text:
Symptom: NaN or Inf values, model crashes mid-run

Solution: - Check forcing data for extreme values - Try reducing timestep - Enable debug mode for more info

docs.title: Memory Issues
docs.text:
Symptom: Segfault, out-of-memory errors

Solution: - Reduce domain size - Increase memory allocation - Check for array bounds issues (enable DEBUG=TRUE)

docs.title: Cycled DATM Forcing Crash (dtlimit)
docs.text:
Symptom: The model hard-crashes at a forcing/stream boundary — often the final timestep or a cycle wrap — with an error originating in dshr_strdata_mod.F90:1050.

Cause: When a DATM stream cycles (taxmode = cycle) and wraps past its last record, the jump in record-time spacing trips CDEPS's default dtlimit = 1.5. This is stock CDEPS behavior, not a data problem — it bites any finite forcing window that is cycled (e.g. the custom NEON OSBS forcing, 2017-02 → 2025-06).

Solution: Set dtlimit = -1 on the affected stream(s) in user_nl_datm_streams — CDEPS's own escape hatch for streams that do not cycle on January boundaries. Namelist-only, no rebuild.

See NEON Atmospheric Forcing for the concrete OSBS case.

docs.title: Runtime Diagnostics (No Rebuild)
docs.text:
./xmlchange INFO_DBUG=2
./case.submit

Adds diagnostic output from the driver and mediator (drv.log, med.log).

docs.title: Full Debug Mode (Requires Rebuild)
docs.text:
./xmlchange DEBUG=TRUE
./case.build --clean-all
./case.build
./case.submit

Enables bounds checking, floating-point exception trapping. Runs much slower.

docs.title: Compilation Errors
docs.text:
Check the build log: 

./xmlquery EXEROOT
cat $EXEROOT/lnd.bldlog.*

Common causes: - Missing modules (run module restore ctsm-modules) - Syntax errors in SourceMods

docs.title: Rebuild After Changes
docs.text:
If you modify source code or build settings: 

./case.build --clean-all
./case.build

docs.title: Timing Analysis
docs.text:
Check simulation performance in med.log:

grep "Model Date" med.log.* | tail -20

Output shows time per model day: 

Model Date: 2018-01-03T00:00:00 wall clock = 2026-07-20T11:38:18 avg dt =     1.07 s/day, dt =     1.09 s/day, rate =   216.87 ypd

  • avg dt = average wall-clock seconds per model day
  • dt = seconds for this specific day
  • rate = simulated years per wall-clock day (ypd)

The end of drv.log also reports overall throughput (# simulated years / cmp-day).

Large variations in dt suggest system performance issues.

docs.title: Corrupted Restarts
docs.text:
If a job timed out while writing restarts, files may be corrupted.

Solution: 1. Check restart file sizes (should be consistent) 2. Remove corrupted files 3. Copy previous restart set 4. Continue from earlier point

# List restart files by size
ls -la $RUNDIR/*.r.*.nc

# Remove potentially corrupted latest set
rm $RUNDIR/*.r.0050-01-01*.nc

# Update rpointer files to point to earlier restart

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
1. Check official docs: CIME Troubleshooting

  2. Search forums: DiscussCESM

  3. Include in bug reports:

  4. CaseStatus file
  5. Relevant log excerpts
  6. Machine and version info
  7. Steps to reproduce

docs.title: Swenson Implementation Overview
docs.text: Custom hillslope parameters for OSBS derived from 1m NEON LIDAR data using the Swenson & Lawrence (2025) representative hillslope methodology.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Swenson & Lawrence (2025) published a global hillslope dataset derived from MERIT DEM at ~90m resolution. This dataset is available independently (not bundled with CTSM) and can be used with CTSM's hillslope hydrology mode. However, Swenson & Lawrence explicitly noted that this resolution "may not be fine enough to capture topographic variations in areas of very low topographic relief, such as wetlands." OSBS is exactly this case — a low-relief wetlandscape where the Terrestrial-Aquatic Interface depends on meter-scale elevation differences.

The goal of this work was to implement Swenson's methodology using 1m NEON LIDAR data to produce custom hillslope parameters that resolve the fine-scale topography controlling wetland-upland transitions at OSBS.

docs.title: Key Differences from Swenson
docs.text: Aspect Swenson (Global) Our Implementation DEM source MERIT (~90m) NEON LIDAR (1m) Coordinate system Geographic (lat/lon) UTM Zone 17N (meters) pysheds version Swenson's fork Our fork (uf-development) with UTM CRS support Processing scope Global tiles Single site (OSBS, 90 km^2) Resolution Direct processing at ~90m Full 1m resolution (no subsampling) Edge handling Not needed (continuous global data) Not needed by construction: domain restricted to the largest 0%-nodata tile rectangle (R4C5-R12C14); the pipeline rejects mosaics containing nodata DTND calculation Hydrological, haversine distance Hydrological, Euclidean distance (UTM-aware pysheds) Lc determination FFT natural peak Restricted-wavelength FFT (min 20m cutoff)

docs.title: Guiding Principle
docs.text: Do not reinvent the wheel. Swenson's paper and codebase served as the template throughout. The implementation followed Swenson's algorithms as closely as possible, deviating only where the change in resolution or coordinate system required adaptation.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
The pipeline was built up incrementally. Early work (December 2025 to January 2026) focused on porting Swenson's pgrid.py to the pysheds fork and reproducing his published MERIT results to verify the port against a published reference, before the phase scheme was introduced. As the OSBS implementation revealed problems that couldn't be solved in a single pass, remaining work was split into discrete phases (A–H) — each addressing a specific blocker. The phases cluster into five groups matching the roadmap in swenson/STATUS.md.

Pre-phase (2025-12 to 2026-01) — Methodology verification. Ported Swenson's pgrid.py to the pysheds fork; the nine-stage MERIT reproduction reached r > 0.95 on five of six parameters by Stage 8. After a 2026-02 post-audit the regression baseline is r > 0.98 on five parameters, with area fraction at 0.92 (up from 0.82).

Phases A–D (2026-02 to 2026-03) — Pipeline foundations. A added UTM CRS support to the pysheds fork so it could process OSBS NEON tiles (EPSG:32617) in projected coordinates; 83 passing unit tests across four fork-written test files (33 upstream tests skipped). B confirmed the full 1 m LIDAR could be processed at 64 GB without subsampling (58 GB peak in the Phase B full-pipeline benchmark on the 90 M-pixel domain; the production run itself peaks at 24 GiB). C established the method for Lc: a restricted-wavelength FFT of the DEM Laplacian with a 20 m cutoff, circumventing the k² artifact that at 1 m puts the spectral peak at ~8 m. On the contiguous mosaic the cutoff sweep gave 356 m (20 and 50 m cutoffs, lognormal) to 285 m (100 m cutoff, Gaussian); the PI accepted ~300 m (range 285–356 m) as the working value on 2026-02-11, and the two physical-plausibility checks were run at 285, 300 and 356 m. Lc is not prescribed: the production pipeline computes it at run time from the FFT (run_pipeline.py fixes only the 20 m cutoff), and on the 90-tile production domain it returns Lc = 355.98 m, the upper end of the Phase C range. Lc is domain-dependent — the same method gives 541 m on the single tile R6C10 and 479 m on the 5 × 5 block — so the production value is specific to R4C5–R12C14. D rebuilt the pipeline with the A/B/C fixes, followed by two internal audit reports: a full pipeline audit with equation-by-equation verification (2026-03-10) and a line-by-line divergence audit against Swenson's original code (2026-03-16). See swenson/audit/260310-osbs_pipeline_and_docs/.

Phase E (2026-03 to 2026-04) — Completing the parameter set. Four decisions were made on the rebuilt pipeline before the bin scheme was redesigned. Slope and aspect were switched from pgrid's Horn stencil to NEON's DP3.30025.001 products (PI-approved 2026-03-23; per-tile comparison against the in-house computation: slope r = 0.91, aspect circular r = 0.84). Open water was masked with NWI polygons (103 Lacustrine and Palustrine Unconsolidated Bottom features, 11.9% of the domain before the E.6 hole-fill). The first integration injected the lake boundaries into the stream network, as Swenson's code does for basins; at 1 m that fragmented the domain from ~800 to 222 K catchments and was replaced on 2026-03-27 by the dual-mask design (natural stream mask for catchment delineation, stream-plus-lake mask for HAND). On 2026-03-30 the PI settled the remaining questions: standard depression filling for D8, the 90-tile domain final, stream parameters left as interim power laws. Binning went through four interim schemes on conditioned HAND — 1 × 8 log-spaced (2026-03-19), 1 × 4 equal-area (03-24), an 8-bin scheme with a 0.1 m noise floor and Q95 log spacing (04-09), and a 16-bin hybrid of five fixed 10 cm bins plus ten log-spaced bins (04-14) — each limited by the same fact: on conditioned HAND about 22% of the land pixels sit at the resolve_flats noise floor, so the lowest bins carried no terrain signal. E.5 removed that limit by binning on raw HAND. Record: swenson/phases/E-complete-parameters.md.

Phases E.5 + E.6 (2026-04 to 2026-05) — Parameter set. E.5 replaced the Phase E conditioned-HAND schemes with the 24-bin TAI-focused scheme (12 flood-zone + 12 upland, 0.25 m floor) and locked raw-HAND binning with Q01/Q99 outlier discard; lake column placement at chain index 1 with hill_elev = −6.0 m. E.6 closed ~400 K interior polygon gaps in the rasterized NWI water mask via scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes.

Phases F + G (2026-05, complete) — Validate and deploy. G Stage 1 completed the submerged lake column and released the production NetCDF hillslopes_osbs_production_c260505.nc on 2026-05-05. Phase F consumed that file: a 600-yr accelerated AD spinup with the operative case osbs.swenson.spinup completed 2026-05-14 and was analyzed 2026-05-19. Three verdicts: convergence PASS (drift_50yr = −0.48%), TAI signal absent (O_SCALAR ≈ 1.0 with anoxia active), lake column stable. The bridge-zone water-table anomaly at chain indices 3–6 was resolved by the PI (2026-08-19); the PI continues to investigate the O_SCALAR anoxia absence (see Current Status below).

Phase H (2026-05) — Stream-side coupling. Track A completed the mesh-mode workaround for CTSM Issue #1432 (see Lateral Flow and Routing) and remains complete and available. Tracks B and C — enabling use_hillslope_routing = .true. — were retired 2026-08-19 (the PI has the routing/drainage situation handled); the 2026-05-19 routing-gate source audit established that inter-column lateral flow already runs under use_hillslope = .true. regardless.

Phase I (2026-07 to 2026-08) — NEON atmospheric forcing. An input-quality upgrade independent of the hillslope parameters: the operative case is driven by 0.5° CRUNCEPv7 reanalysis, which discards the on-site NEON flux-tower record (including measured incident longwave). A fork of the NCAR-NEON pipeline, run offline on HiPerGator, produced a site-native OSBS forcing dataset — 101 monthly DATM files spanning 2017-02 → 2025-06, verified against the pre-built NCAR-NEON v4 product and shown to drive a stable, converged AD spinup. It is engineering-complete and handed to the PI for adoption. See NEON Atmospheric Forcing.

Detailed phase records: swenson/phases/ in the hpg-esm-tools repo.

The pipeline produces the OSBS production hillslope file hillslopes_osbs_production_c260505.nc — 25 columns (1 lake at chain index 1 + 24 land bins) on a single aspect, computed over the R4C5–R12C14 production domain (90 tiles, 9 × 10 km, 0% nodata, 1 m resolution). They are stored in the NetCDF for completeness; under the operative use_hillslope_routing=.false. configuration, none of these values are read by CTSM (Lateral Flow and Routing).

docs.title: Parameter Comparison
docs.text:
The two datasets have different column structures and cannot be compared aspect-by-aspect. The OSBS production file uses a single omnidirectional aspect with 24 HAND bins plus a dedicated lake column; the Swenson global file uses Swenson's default 4 × 4 partition. Values below summarize column-level statistics from each file. Sources: OSBS production hillslope_params.json and production_summary.txt; Swenson NetCDF.

Parameter Swenson (Global) OSBS (Current) Aspects × HAND bins 4 × 4 1 × 24 Lake column None Chain index 1, hill_elev = −6.0 m, hill_area ≈ 11.08 km² (NWI aggregate) Hillslope-element HAND range (m) 0.17 — 8.14 −5.13 — 12.46 (land bins; lake at −6.0) Hillslope-element distance range (m) 67 — 541 2.6 — 353 (land bins; lake at 1.3) Stream-network slope (m/m) 0.00233 0.00690 Lc (m) not stored in file 356 Stream cells, fraction of domain n/a (gridcell aggregate) 0.15% (1m resolution)

The OSBS file's negative HAND values are real terrain — pixels in filled depressions where raw HAND (conditioned HAND minus the depression-fill depth) is below zero. The 24-bin scheme bins on raw HAND so that flood-zone columns retain their submerged character rather than being clipped to zero by the depression fill. See HAND Binning and Lake Column for the Q01/Q99 outlier-trim derivation and per-bin area allocation.

docs.title: Key Observations
docs.text:
1. Distance scales differ most at the stream end. Swenson distances range 67-541 m; OSBS land-bin distances range 2.6-353 m. The ridge-end values differ by ~1.5× (541 vs 353 m); the stream-end values differ by ~26× (67 vs 2.6 m) because the OSBS chain begins inside filled depressions adjacent to the wide water mask. This is much closer than previous (pre-fix) runs showed (5-25× difference) because the current pipeline uses hydrological DTND (distance to the drainage-linked stream pixel) rather than EDT (distance to the geographically nearest stream pixel). The remaining difference is consistent with the denser stream network resolved at 1 m (Lc = 356 m), which produces more stream pixels per unit area. Swenson's file does not record the Lc used for this gridcell, so the two Lc values cannot be compared directly.

2. Land-bin slopes are systematically higher at 1 m than 90 m. Full 1 m resolution captures local topographic variability that 90 m MERIT averages away. This is expected — slope is the most resolution-sensitive of the six parameters (Phase B confirmed systematic underestimation at coarser resolution, ~50% reduction at 4 m vs 1 m in the lowest HAND bin).

3. Negative HAND values appear in the OSBS file. Swenson's MERIT-derived file has only positive HANDs (0.17-8.14 m). The OSBS production file has 12 flood-zone bins covering −5.13-0 m HAND because the 1 m LIDAR resolves real terrain below the depression-filled drainage network (depressions, swales, lake margins). These bins are physically meaningful at OSBS — the saturation gradient through the flood zone is the TAI signal the column structure is designed to resolve.

4. The OSBS file has a dedicated lake column. The Swenson global file has no lake representation; lake area is implicit in the gridcell-aggregated parameters. The OSBS file places all NWI open water (≈ 11.08 km², ~12% of the production domain) in a separate column at chain index 1, so that two-way water exchange between the lake and adjacent land bins is explicit in the CTSM column chain.

5. The aspect partition is collapsed at OSBS. Swenson's 4-aspect default expresses the difference between sun-facing and shaded hillslopes. At OSBS, with bin slopes of 0.04-0.07 m/m, aspect-dependent insolation has little physical impact (a few percent of incident solar at midday sun angles), so the same 24 HAND bins serve every direction and the aspect dimension is collapsed to 1.

docs.title: OSBS (Current — 1m NEON LIDAR)
docs.text:
OSBS elevation and width profiles across 25 columns (1 lake at chain index 1 + 24 land bins) on a single aspect. Lake column marked with a blue star; flood-zone bins (raw HAND < 0) in dark red; upland bins in green.

The elevation curve is smooth from the lake column (HAND = −6.0 m at ~1.3 m from the stream) through the 12 flood-zone bins, crossing zero between ~50 and ~62 m, and rising to the ridge (+12.5 m at ~353 m). The width curve tapers from ~555 m near the stream to ~270 m at the ridge, following the trapezoidal plan-form fit. Contrast with Swenson's four-aspect profiles above, which lack the flood-zone segment — MERIT 90 m data cannot resolve HAND below the depression-filled drainage network.

docs.title: OSBS (Current — 1m NEON LIDAR)
docs.text:
OSBS per-representative column areas across 25 columns. Lake (light blue), flood zone (dark red), upland (green).

The distribution is heavily non-uniform: the lake column alone holds 12.3% of per-rep area (matching the wtlunit ≈ 12.3% design derived from the NWI footprint), the 12 flood-zone bins take small slices (0.7–2.9%) because the TAI-focused fine binning concentrates resolution where terrain area is scarce, and the 12 upland bins are broader (3.6–8.0%). Contrast with Swenson's global 4 × 4 partition above, where the equal-area algorithm smooths the distribution across all 16 columns.

docs.title: Implications for CTSM Simulations
docs.text:
1. Lateral flow dynamics. Shorter hillslope distances (2.6-353 m vs 67-541 m) mean faster lateral water redistribution between columns. The shorter flow paths reduce the response time of the inter-column Darcy gradient (SoilHydrologyMod.F90), which runs whenever use_hillslope=.true. independent of the routing toggle (Lateral Flow and Routing).

2. Hydraulic gradients. The 24-bin scheme is denser in HAND space near the stream channel and lake margin than the 4-bin equal-area default; adjacent-bin elevation differences are sub-meter through the TAI core (0.25 m bin width × terrain-driven HAND increments). Combined with the dedicated lake column at chain index 1, the column chain captures the wet-to-dry gradient at the LIDAR noise floor.

3. TAI representation. Phase F deploys this file in osbs.swenson.spinup under use_hillslope=.true., use_hillslope_routing=.false.. Inter-column lateral flow between flood-zone bins and adjacent land bins is active in this configuration; Phase H Tracks B/C (which would have added the CTSM-internal stream-channel boundary condition at the chain terminus) were retired 2026-08-19.

4. Column weighting. OSBS column weights are calibrated by the per-rep rescaling: nhill_implicit ≈ 533 rep-hillslope copies per landunit, with the lake column at wtlunit ≈ 12.3%. The land bins partition the remainder according to their NWI-masked, water-excluded pixel areas. See HAND Binning and Lake Column for the rescaling derivation.

docs.title: HAND Binning and Lake Column
docs.text: The OSBS production hillslope file departs from the Swenson default 4-aspect × 4-elevation-bin structure in two coupled ways: a 24-bin TAI-focused HAND scheme replaces the 4-bin equal-area partition, and a dedicated lake column at chain index 1 represents aggregated NWI open water. The two changes are documented together because the bin scheme and the lake column are co-designed — the lake anchors the bottom of the chain and the lowest land bin sits just above it.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
The Swenson global methodology bins HAND so each elevation bin holds approximately the same number of pixels per aspect, with a mandatory 2 m upper bound on the lowest bin. On flat terrain this produces near-zero lowest-bin mean HAND — earlier OSBS runs at 4 bins × 4 aspects gave Q25 = 0.00027 m for the lowest bin, because 25% of the production-domain pixels have HAND below LIDAR noise. A bin whose mean elevation sits at the LIDAR noise floor cannot resolve the saturation gradient that defines the terrestrial-aquatic interface.

The 24-bin scheme addresses this by tilting bin resolution toward the TAI and lifting the bin-width floor to the LIDAR vertical noise budget.

HAND map of the production domain (R4C5-R12C14, 9 × 10 km, 1 m). Dark purple is low HAND (near streams and flood-zone interiors); bright yellow is upland ridge; white pixels are NWI open water excluded from land bins. The TAI is the color band where the saturation gradient is steepest — the 24-bin scheme concentrates bin resolution there.

docs.title: 24-bin TAI-focused scheme
docs.text:
The production scheme uses 24 bins total: 12 flood-zone bins (HAND < 0 m, set by the depression-filled reference DEM) plus 12 upland bins (HAND ≥ 0 m). The width allocation tilts toward the TAI core:

Bin range Width Count Deep tail sentinel 2.35 m 1 Deeper flood zone 1.0 m 1 Deep flood-zone TAI 0.5 m 2 TAI core (flood-zone + stream margin) 0.25 m 10 Inner upland TAI 0.5 m 3 Mid upland 1.0 m 4 Mid-to-ridge 2.0 m 2 Ridge sentinel ~7 m 1

The geometric width progression outward from the TAI core (0.25 m → 0.5 m → 1.0 m → 2.0 m → ~7 m) tracks the attenuation of TAI process gradients into the terrestrial realm: saturation, biogeochemistry, and vegetation transitions are sharpest near the wet/dry boundary and smooth into nominal upland tens of meters away.

docs.title: Why 0.25 m as the bin-width floor
docs.text:
NEON specifies an absolute vertical accuracy of ≤ 0.15 m RMSE for its bare-earth LIDAR DTM (NEON Lidar collection). Raw HAND is a difference between nearby pixels, so what matters is relative noise, which an estimated error budget puts at:

Step Estimate Absolute → relative pixel noise (shared biases cancel; ~0.6 × 0.15 m) 0.09 m Bare-earth gridding noise, typical mixed pine/sandhill pixel (in quadrature) ~0.07 m → 0.11 m per pixel HAND differencing (√2, partly offset by shared flight-line errors) ~0.12 m DEM conditioning (fill_pits, resolve_flats; in quadrature) ~0.03 m → σ(raw HAND) ≈ 0.12 m

σ(raw HAND) ranges from ~0.08 m (open sandhill) to ~0.15-0.18 m (wetland edges); these factors are estimates, not measurements. Using the standard 2σ rule for distinguishing two populations, 2σ ≈ 0.24 m, rounded to a 0.25 m floor. The concern is pixel membership: with bins narrower than this, noise rather than terrain would decide which side of a bin edge a pixel falls on. The large pixel counts per bin make bin means precise, but they do not fix misassignment near edges. 0.25 m also sits at the low end of the OSBS capillary-fringe range (30-60 cm), so adjacent bins represent roughly distinct hydrologic regimes. The floor is implemented as hard-coded bin edges in compute_hand_bins_tai_focused (hillslope_params.py). Full derivation: Phase E.5.

docs.title: Why we accept non-monotonic bin areas
docs.text: Swenson's bin algorithm targets approximately equal per-bin areas; CTSM imposes no monotonicity requirement on hill_area. The 24-bin scheme allows bin areas to vary with terrain heterogeneity. The smoothness criterion used instead is per-meter pixel density (area ÷ bin width): the density curve rises smoothly to a peak and tapers, tracking the underlying HAND distribution. The production scheme's per-meter density rises from 0.62 km²/m at the deepest sentinel to a peak of 13.9 km²/m at bin 13 (just above stream level, where OSBS pixel density peaks) and tapers smoothly to 0.92 km²/m at the ridge sentinel. The density curve is monotonic toward the peak from each side — the physically meaningful invariant for gridcell aggregation.

docs.title: Outlier handling
docs.text:
Q01 (raw HAND) = −6.35 m and Q99 = +17.02 m define the binning envelope for the production domain. Pixels outside this envelope are discarded, not clipped into sentinel bins, for two reasons:

  1. Both tails are real terrain. The outlier diagnostic (2026-05-01, run on the 2026-04-24 diagnostic arrays, i.e. before the E.6 hole-fill, when the cutoffs were −6.34 / +17.46 m) shows the sharpest density breaks at Q01 (33.5× density step) and Q99 (34.8×), with negligible singleton mass beyond; the ratios were not recomputed after E.6 moved Q99 to 17.02 m. The tails are not isolated noise pixels; they are continuous topography that would inflate sentinel-bin weights if retained.
  2. Clipping into sentinel bins would force the deepest pit and ridge extrema to share a bin with a much larger area of moderately deep / high terrain, distorting both the mean HAND and the gridcell-aggregated mass-and-energy balance for those bins.

The discard removes ~1.5 M pixels (~2% of the production-domain land area).

Binning is performed on raw HAND rather than conditioned HAND (which is ≥ 0 by construction). Raw HAND is conditioned HAND minus the depression-fill depth, hand − (flooded_orig − pit_filled): in effect, a pixel's pit-filled elevation minus the elevation of the stream or open-water cell it drains to, negative inside filled depressions. Raw HAND preserves the depth of pixels in filled depressions, which is the physically relevant quantity for the flood-zone bins; conditioned HAND would force every below-stream pixel to HAND = 0, collapsing the FZ side of the chain.

docs.title: Water masking strategy
docs.text:
Two water masks are computed and used at different stages:

Mask Coverage Used for Narrow stream mask Pixels above the accumulation threshold (A_thresh = int(0.5 × Lc²) = 63,362 pixels at 1 m, with Lc = 355.98 m) Catchment delineation, flow-accumulation arithmetic, network density Wide water mask Stream mask ∪ NWI open-water polygons (Lacustrine + Palustrine Unconsolidated Bottom) Exclusion from HAND binning and DTND statistics; aggregated into the lake column

The wide mask ensures that lake-surface pixels do not contaminate land-bin HAND statistics: an NWI-identified lake has water-surface elevation that, in HAND terms, is whatever the depression-fill algorithm filled the lake to (usually a uniform fill level). Counting those pixels into land bins would skew the lowest land bins toward zero HAND, undoing the TAI signal the 24-bin scheme is designed to resolve.

docs.title: NWI mask hole-fill
docs.text: Raw NWI polygons (from the USFWS NWI HUC8 03080103 "Lower St. John" watershed extract, October 2024 database version, 2017 true-colour imagery) miss interior holes that the 1 m LIDAR confirms are contiguous open water: small islands inside larger features, sub-polygon gaps where the digitizer missed thin shore strips, and mis-aligned edges. A scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes pass over the rasterized NWI mask closes approximately 400,000 pixels of these holes. The hole-fill is applied before the mask is used downstream (wide-mask construction, lake-area aggregation, perimeter computation).

docs.title: Lake column construction
docs.text:
The OSBS production file places a dedicated lake column at chain index 1, shifting land columns to indices 2-25. The lake column represents the aggregate of all NWI open water in the production domain as a single submerged element.

Field Value Rationale column_index 1 Lake at chain bottom. Preserves the PI's SourceMod loop structure (terminal-column gate at cold == ispval) by keeping the lake first in the SurfaceWaterMod iteration. downhill_column_index -9999 Terminal column (drains to stream channel under routing-on; bounded by tdepth_grc under routing-off). hillslope_index 1 Same single aspect as the 24 land bins. hill_elev −6.0 m Chain-bookkeeping value, 0.87 m below the deepest land bin's mean (−5.13 m) to keep the chain monotonic. Not a physical lake bottom; see note below. hill_distance 0.5 × Bin 1 distance = 1.30 m (Bin 1 = 2.59 m) Keeps the Bin 1 → lake distance difference positive by construction; see note below. hill_area Σ(water_mask × pixel_area) ≈ 11.08 km² (11,082,394 px; rescaled per rep to ≈ 0.021 km²) Total NWI-masked water area in the production domain after hole-fill. The binary_fill_holes step adds ~400,000 interior pixels to the 10.68 km² pre-fill mask, giving 11.08 km². Production domain has 103 NWI water features. hill_width 0.5 × NWI total perimeter ≈ 48,270 m (rescaled per rep to ≈ 90 m) PI direction (2026-04-25). Half the perimeter approximates the effective lateral exchange surface between the lake and its land-facing margin. Inert under the operative routing-off configuration. hill_slope 0 Water surface is horizontal. hill_aspect 0 Inconsequential for the flat lake column. hill_bedrock_depth 0 Matches the hillslope convention; inert under CTSM's Uniform soil profile method.

Lake hill_elev. Empirical lake bathymetry from NWI digitizing and Lee 2023 spill-stage data is far shallower than −6.0 m (NWI mean ~−2.5 m, Lee/pipeline spill 2.6-3.3 m), but the deepest land bin's HAND (−5.13 m) is the binding constraint on monotonicity. PI direction (2026-05-04): tuning the lake elevation toward a physical lake depth is deferred to model-output review; chain integrity comes first.

Lake hill_distance. The inter-column Darcy gradient in SoilHydrologyMod.F90 divides by the distance difference hill_distance(c) − hill_distance(cold(c)) for interior columns (Bin 1 → lake: 2.59 − 1.30 = 1.30 m) and by hill_distance(c) for the terminal lake column. The difference must stay positive. Bin 1's trapezoid-fit distance at OSBS is small, so a static lake distance of ~5 m would invert the gradient sign. Deriving the lake distance as half of Bin 1's guarantees positivity.

Four hillslope parameters across the 25 columns of the production NetCDF: mean raw HAND (top-left), mean DTND (top-right), per-rep hillslope element area (bottom-left), and lower-edge width (bottom-right). The chain is ordered lake → deepest flood-zone bin (1) → ridge bin (24). Color-coded: lake (light blue), flood zone with raw HAND < 0 (dark red), upland with raw HAND ≥ 0 (green). The HAND chain rises monotonically from −6.0 m at the lake to +12.5 m at the ridge bin. DTND grows smoothly from ~1.3 m at the lake to ~353 m at the ridge. Area is small in the flood zone (narrow bins resolve the TAI core) and largest in mid-upland (where bin widths broaden). Width is set by the trapezoidal plan-form fit and is largest near the stream-margin bins.

docs.title: Design history
docs.text:
The lake column reached its production form through five revisions in four weeks, recorded in phases/G-ctsm-lake-representation.md and phases/E.5-bin-redesign.md:

  • 2026-04-09 — weir overflow abandoned. The first production NetCDF was generated the same day the PI reviewed a plan to represent lakes by repurposing CTSM's stream-channel fields as lake geometry with weir overflow; the plan was dropped.
  • 2026-04-10 — submerged column. Phase G pivoted to a lake column inside the hillslope chain, at first framed around the runtime spillheight offset. A CTSM source audit (2026-04-21 to 04-24) established how hill_distance enters the Darcy gradient, that the column belongs at chain index 1, and that hill_bedrock_depth is inert under the Uniform soil-profile method.
  • 2026-04-25 — scope narrowed to NWI open water. Earlier framing had absorbed every depression-filled pixel into the lake; the PI limited the column to mapped open water, set hill_width to half the NWI perimeter and hill_slope to 0, and declined to force permanent submersion. The unmapped depressions became the flood-zone bins of Phase E.5.
  • 2026-04-30 — spillheight retired (see SPILLHEIGHT: the retired runtime offset).
  • 2026-05-04 — elevation locked, distance bug fixed. hill_elev was set to −6.0 m as a chain-bookkeeping value (see Lake hill_elev above). The first production run under raw-HAND binning (c260504) carried a static 5 m hill_distance, which made the Bin 1 → lake Darcy denominator negative (2.59 − 5 = −2.41 m): the deepest bin's fitted distance is far smaller under raw HAND than the ~30 m the audit had assumed. The dynamic 0.5 × Bin 1 rule replaced it the same day.
  • 2026-05-05 — per-rep rescale. Inspection of that file showed the lake area in total-NWI units (11.08 km²) against land bins in Swenson's per-representative-hillslope units (0.148 km² in all), which would have given the lake 98.7% of the landunit weight. Rescaling the lake by the implicit hillslope count (≈534) brought it to 12.3%, the NWI fraction of the domain, and produced the production file c260505 (next section).

docs.title: Per-rep rescaling
docs.text:
The lake-column area (11.08 km²) is far larger than any single representative hillslope's footprint, because OSBS open water is the aggregate of 103 NWI features distributed across the 90 km² production domain. To fit the column inside a representative-hillslope shape, the pipeline computes:

  • nhill_implicit — the implicit number of representative-hillslope copies that tile the gridcell. For the 2026-05-05 production: nhill_implicit ≈ 533.7.
  • Per-rep area = total area / nhill_implicit. Lake column per rep: 11.08 km² / 533.7 ≈ 0.021 km² = 20,765 m².
  • Per-rep width = hill_width / nhill_implicit. Lake per rep: 48,270 m / 533.7 ≈ 90.4 m. (hill_width = 48,270 m is half the total NWI perimeter of 96,540 m.)

Within the representative hillslope, the lake column ends up with wtlunit ≈ 12.3%, calibrated to the NWI water footprint as a fraction of the production domain (~12% open water). The land bins partition the remaining 87.7% according to their NWI-masked, water-excluded pixel areas.

docs.title: First approach: a runtime elevation offset (November 2025 to April 2026)
docs.text:
Before Phase E.5, the pipeline binned on conditioned HAND — the depression-filled DEM's elevation above stream. Conditioned HAND is zero or positive by construction: pixels inside filled depressions sit at the depression's fill level, not below it. Equal-area binning on this signal produced no flood-zone columns; the lowest land bin's mean HAND landed at LIDAR noise (Q25 = 0.00027 m on earlier 4-bin runs), as documented in the Motivation section.

To represent the wet, low-lying terrain visible in the NEON LIDAR, the PI's CTSM SourceMods instead created wetland columns at run time. A spillheight parameter in the HillslopeHydrologyMod.F90 SourceMod (default 0.2 m; osbs2.branch.spillheight used 0.5 m) was subtracted from every column's hill_elev as the hillslope file was read, lowering the whole chain so that the lowest land bins fell below the stream reference, and a companion rule in the SurfaceWaterMod.F90 SourceMod let columns with a negative elevation pond rather than drain. The lake column was placed in the file at hill_elev = −spillheight so that it became the permanently submerged anchor of the chain. The CTSM fork added spillheight to the hillslope namelist group (namelist_definition_ctsm.xml, 2026-01-12) so that the offset could be set from user_nl_clm instead of by editing the SourceMod.

docs.title: Why raw-HAND binning superseded it (PI decision, 2026-04-30)
docs.text:
Phase E.5 switched the pipeline's binning input from conditioned HAND to raw HAND (conditioned HAND minus the depression-fill depth, signed; see Outlier handling). Raw HAND preserves the depression-fill depth as a negative HAND value, so flood-zone columns emerge from the data:

  • The deepest land bin (chain index 2 in the production NetCDF) has a mean HAND of −5.13 m.
  • Eleven additional flood-zone bins (chain indices 3 through 13) resolve the saturation gradient up to HAND = 0.
  • The lake column carries its own chain-bookkeeping elevation, hill_elev = −6.0 m (locked 2026-05-04; see Lake column construction above), in place of the earlier −spillheight convention.
  • The bin areas, per-meter density, and Darcy-relevant geometry all derive from the original LIDAR rather than from a runtime offset applied to the file.

A uniform offset cannot do this: it lowers every column by the same amount, whereas raw-HAND binning gives each column the depth the LIDAR actually shows below its drainage reference. The 2026-04-30 PI meeting therefore retired the offset; the depths it was meant to impose at run time are now in the file.

docs.title: Status: the parameter is dead
docs.text:
The offset is disabled in every production case through the namelist:

spillheight = 0.0

This line is present in osbs5.swenson.spinup, osbs.swenson.spinup, osbs.swenson.post-ad, and osbs.swenson.neon.spinup, and at zero the subtraction is an identity. The PI subsequently removed the spillheight parameter from his own SourceMods altogether (first in osbs5-1, 2026-05-19); his CTSM tree never carried the fork's namelist entry. The parameter therefore no longer exists outside the fork's namelist definition and the user_nl_clm override that keeps it at zero.

docs.title: What the runtime reads from the file
docs.text: The SourceMods are run-time modifications to CTSM; they never touch the pipeline, the bin edges, or the NetCDF, and the pipeline reads nothing from CTSM. The one interface between the two is the sign of hill_elev: the hillslope physics identifies wetland columns as those with hill_elev < 0, so the twelve negative-HAND flood-zone bins and the −6.0 m lake column are what the model treats as wetland. The binning determines which columns are wetland; the runtime does not alter the binning.

docs.title: Lateral Flow and Routing
docs.text: CTSM hillslope mode is controlled by two related-but-distinct namelist toggles. This page documents what each one activates physically, based on a 2026-05-19 source-code audit of CTSM 5.3.085. The distinction is consequential: prior project framing conflated the two, and the operative osbs.swenson.spinup configuration is built on the corrected understanding.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CTSM 5.3 exposes two namelist toggles for hillslope-mode physics:

use_hillslope         = .true.    ! activates hillslope-mode column structure
use_hillslope_routing = .true.    ! activates stream-side machinery (optional)

A 2026-05-19 audit of CTSM 5.3.085 (tag ctsm5.3.085, fde1fc622; the Fortran under src/ is identical in our fork revision dc3aa5ddc) traced every source-code site gated by use_hillslope_routing and cross-checked the conclusions against empirical output from two cases: a 5-yr paired test/control smoke test (mesh-mode workaround validation, Phase H Track A) and the 600-yr accelerated AD spinup of the operative case. The audit established that inter-column lateral subsurface flow runs under use_hillslope = .true. and does not require routing to be on. Routing-on activates only the stream-side coupling at the chain terminus.

docs.title: Inter-column lateral subsurface flow
docs.text:
HydrologyDrainageMod.F90:127-160 dispatches the lateral-flow routines outside any routing gate:

if (use_aquifer_layer()) then
   call Drainage(...)                          ! aquifer-layer mode (not used at OSBS)
else
   call PerchedLateralFlow(...)                ! ALWAYS, no routing gate
   call SubsurfaceLateralFlow(...)             ! ALWAYS, no routing gate
   if (use_hillslope_routing) then
      call HillslopeStreamOutflow(...)         ! routing-gated
      call HillslopeUpdateStreamWater(...)     ! routing-gated
   endif
endif

The OSBS case takes the else branch (lower_boundary_condition=2 → bc_zero_flux → use_aquifer_layer() = .false.; see bld/namelist_files/namelist_defaults_ctsm.xml:448 and SoilWaterMovementMod.F90:229). PerchedLateralFlow and SubsurfaceLateralFlow are therefore called every hydrology step regardless of routing.

docs.title: The Darcy gradient between adjacent columns
docs.text:
SubsurfaceLateralFlow (SoilHydrologyMod.F90:2086+) is the canonical inter-column water-table flow routine. Its main loop at :2249-2402 processes every active hillslope column. Inside the loop, two paths:

Internal columns (those with a downhill neighbor, col%cold(c) /= ispval):

! Darcy head gradient at :2261-2263
head_gradient = (col%hill_elev(c) - zwt(c)) &
              - (col%hill_elev(col%cold(c)) - zwt(col%cold(c)))
head_gradient = head_gradient / (col%hill_distance(c) - col%hill_distance(col%cold(c)))

The denominator is the distance between the column and its downhill neighbor, so hill_distance must increase monotonically up the chain.

The outflow volume at :2358 is qflx_latflow_out_vol = transmissivity × col%hill_width(c) × head_gradient. The downhill column accumulates the inflow at :2386-2388. No routing gate anywhere in this path.

Terminal column (the chain bottom, col%cold(c) == ispval): the same Darcy machinery, but the "downhill neighbor" is the stream channel, and the head difference is divided by the column's own distance, col%hill_distance(c) (:2280). Routing matters here for the stream-depth source — see the next section.

PerchedLateralFlow (:1703+) is structurally identical for the perched water table, using zwt_perched: the interior gradient at :1817-1820 divides by the same distance difference, and the terminal branch at :1838 divides by col%hill_distance(c).

docs.title: Where the flow is applied to soil water
docs.text:
SubsurfaceLateralFlow at :2433-2509:

qflx_net_latflow(c) = qflx_latflow_out(c) - qflx_latflow_in(c)
...
drainage(c) = qflx_net_latflow(c)                  ! for hillslope columns
...
drainage_tot = - drainage(c) * dtime
if (drainage_tot > 0.) then                         ! rising water table
   ! water added to h2osoi_liq, zwt rises
else                                                ! deepening water table
   ! water removed from h2osoi_liq, zwt falls
endif

A column that receives more lateral inflow than it sends out gets negative drainage, positive drainage_tot, and water added to h2osoi_liq. The transfer is real and applied to the soil-water state every step.

docs.title: What use_hillslope_routing = .true. additionally activates
docs.text:
Twelve source-code sites are gated by use_hillslope_routing in CTSM 5.3.085 (excluding declaration, broadcast, and log plumbing). Every one is on the stream-channel side of the column chain; none are inside the column-to-column flow path of PerchedLateralFlow or SubsurfaceLateralFlow.

File:line What it gates HillslopeHydrologyMod.F90:378-411 Read hillslope_stream_depth/width/slope from the NetCDF HillslopeHydrologyMod.F90:475-507 Compute nhill_per_landunit, stream_channel_length, stream_channel_number HillslopeHydrologyMod.F90:1053+ (HillslopeUpdateStreamWater, called only from HydrologyDrainageMod.F90:150-158) Advance stream_water_volume HillslopeHydrologyMod.F90:939+ (HillslopeStreamOutflow, called only from HydrologyDrainageMod.F90:151-153) Manning's-equation streamflow velocity SoilHydrologyMod.F90:1822-1829 Perched-LF stream-depth source switch (internal ledger vs MOSART) SoilHydrologyMod.F90:2265-2272 Subsurface-LF stream-depth source switch (internal ledger vs MOSART) SoilHydrologyMod.F90:2362-2367 Losing-stream outflow cap WaterFluxType.F90:525-534 Register VOLUMETRIC_STREAMFLOW history field WaterFluxType.F90:922-928 Zero volumetric_streamflow_lun each step BalanceCheckMod.F90:274-280, 744-750 Add stream_water_volume / qflx_streamflow_grc into gridcell water-balance ledger lnd2atmMod.F90:343+ Sum streamflow over landunits for lnd→rof coupling lnd_import_export.F90:916-919 Add stream component to subsurface-runoff field exported to coupler

docs.title: The stream-depth source swap
docs.text:
The single physically-meaningful difference inside the lateral-flow code path is the stream-depth source at the terminal column. SoilHydrologyMod.F90:2265-2272:

if (use_hillslope_routing) then
   stream_water_depth   = stream_water_volume(l) / &
                          lun%stream_channel_length(l) / &
                          lun%stream_channel_width(l)
   stream_channel_depth = lun%stream_channel_depth(l)
else
   stream_water_depth   = tdepth(g)               ! from MOSART via coupler
   stream_channel_depth = tdepth_bankfull(g)      ! from MOSART via coupler
endif

Routing-on uses an internal stream-water ledger updated each step by HillslopeUpdateStreamWater; routing-off uses MOSART's tdepth_grc, supplied via the coupler. The Darcy gradient at the terminal column is computed against some stream depth in both branches; only the source differs.

docs.title: Empirical confirmation
docs.text:
Two observations from our own runs are consistent with active inter-column flow under use_hillslope_routing = .false.. Negative column drainage (QDRAI) is the direct signature: in CTSM 5.3 hillslope columns, drainage equals net lateral outflow (qflx_latflow_out − qflx_latflow_in), so a negative value means net lateral inflow.

  1. Routing.test vs routing.control 5-yr smoke test (2026-05-12). QDRAI has negative values at hillslope columns in both the routing-on (osbs.routing.test) and routing-off (osbs.routing.control) cases. Min/max range is essentially identical: test = −4.32×10⁻⁵ / 1.47×10⁻⁵ mm/s; control = −4.15×10⁻⁵ / 1.43×10⁻⁵ mm/s. The lateral-flow signature is present whether routing is on or off; the values differ only at the ~10⁻⁶ scale (the boundary-condition delta).

  2. osbs.swenson.spinup h1a (600-yr AD, routing-off). Column-level QRUNOFF min/max = −1.156×10⁻⁴ / 1.992×10⁻⁴ mm/s. ZWT spans 0.011 → 8.6 m across the column chain. If hillslope columns were hydrologically isolated 1-D soil columns receiving the same atmospheric forcing, there would be no negative column-level QRUNOFF and far less ZWT variation. Negative column QRUNOFF is consistent with lateral inflow exceeding outflow at the receiving column, though QRUNOFF also includes other terms, so QDRAI (item 1) is the cleaner signal. The ZWT spread is suggestive only, since columns also differ in elevation-downscaled forcing.

docs.title: Implication for the OSBS configuration
docs.text:
The operative case osbs.swenson.spinup runs:

use_hillslope         = .true.
use_hillslope_routing = .false.

with the 2026-05-05 production hillslope file (25 columns: 1 lake + 24 land bins on a single aspect). In this configuration, inter-column lateral subsurface flow is active between all 25 columns of the chain: Darcy gradients redistribute water from upland bins through the flood-zone bins to the lake column, and the terminal-column boundary condition at the lake is supplied by MOSART's tdepth_grc. In this case that value is zero by configuration, not by assumption: the driver flag flds_r2l_stream_channel_depths is .false. in nuopc.runconfig, so MOSART never exports the channel-depth fields and CTSM takes the tdepth_grc = 0 fallback (lnd_import_export.F90:623); MOSART itself runs in NULL mode (MOSART_MODE = NULL) in this single-point case and performs no routing. The chain-bottom boundary is therefore an empty stream channel.

A 600-yr accelerated AD spinup using this configuration completed 2026-05-14 and was analyzed 2026-05-19. Three verdicts: convergence PASS (drift_50yr = −0.48%), TAI signal absent (O_SCALAR ≈ 1.0), lake column stable.

Phase H Tracks B and C would enable use_hillslope_routing = .true. and switch the terminal-column boundary to the internal stream_water_volume ledger. They were retired 2026-08-19 — the PI has the routing/drainage situation handled. The routing-on machinery is built and validated (Track A, below) but is not deployed.

docs.title: CTSM Issue #1432 and the mesh-mode workaround
docs.text:
Status: built and validated, not deployed

The mesh-mode workaround described below is complete and verified but is not active in the operative osbs.swenson.spinup configuration. Issue #1432 only bites when use_hillslope_routing = .true.; the operative case runs with routing off, so grc%area = spval never reaches a live computation. Phase H Track A built and validated the workaround so it is ready if Tracks B/C later enable routing.

docs.title: The bug
docs.text:
In single-point NUOPC mode, grc%area is initialized to spval (~1×10³⁶) at src/cpl/share_esmf/lnd_set_decomp_and_domain.F90:342:

ldomain%area(1) = spval

and propagated to grc%area(g) via initGridCellsMod.F90:179. The value is never repopulated. Under use_hillslope_routing = .false., the routing gate at HillslopeHydrologyMod.F90:475 protects every downstream use of grc%area, so the spval does not corrupt any computation.

Under routing-on, the same gate becomes a release valve. HillslopeHydrologyMod.F90:486-487:

nhill_per_landunit(nh) = grc%area(g) * 1.e6_r8 * lun%wtgcell(l) &
     * pct_hillslope(l,nh) * 0.01 / hillslope_area(nh)

With grc%area = spval, nhill_per_landunit ≈ 1×10³⁶ — physically nonsense, but no error is raised because CTSM has no defensive guards on grc%area. stream_channel_length inherits the 1e36 magnitude at :501-502, and from there every downstream stream-side computation produces garbage in silence.

This is canonical CTSM Issue #1432 (open since 2021-07-20). The community has not encountered it in practice because Swenson's published hillslope users run gridded (the validated mode), and single-point users have run with routing off.

docs.title: The mesh-mode workaround
docs.text:
Replace the PTS_LAT / PTS_LON single-column shortcut with an explicit single-cell ESMF mesh (LND_DOMAIN_MESH). CTSM's mode-decision logic then routes through lnd_set_decomp_and_domain_from_readmesh instead of lnd_set_decomp_and_domain_for_single_column, and ldomain%area is populated from the mesh via ESMF_FieldRegridGetArea() — a real number, not spval.

Swenson recommends this workaround to single-point users. CTSM's shipped mesh_maker tool (python/ctsm/mesh_maker.py, wrapped by tools/site_and_regional/mesh_maker) aborts on 1×1 input (mesh_maker.py:214-216), so Phase H Track A wrote make_osbs_scrip.py (swenson/scripts/osbs/) to produce a single-cell SCRIP-format NetCDF; the prebuilt ESMF_Scrip2Unstruct binary then converts it to the ESMF mesh CTSM reads.

Phase H Track A (2026-05-11 to 2026-05-12) built the single-cell ESMF mesh for the production domain, the supporting input file conversions (surface dataset reformat, domain mesh), and a paired test/control case configuration. The 2026-05-12 smoke test confirmed grc%area = 90.006 km² (matching the production domain area, not spval) under mesh mode; gridcell aggregates are bit-identical between the mesh-mode test and the production-mode control. The workaround is OSBS-side; no upstream CTSM PR is planned.
